description: We are Team Nexorion, a group of passionate computer science students building an immersive, gamified web app for the "Build A Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. We specialize in front-end development, interactive logic, and problem-solving. We are looking for creative teammates with a knack for UI/UX design, gamification mechanics, or educational content creation. Join us if you want to build a fun, out-of-this-world learning experience for future astronauts!
summary:
Red Horizon is an interactive 3D Moon and Mars survival game that works as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for kids aged 7 to 12. Players start with a cinematic launch from Earth, then land on Mars and learn through five guided tutorial levels before surviving 150 Martian days in an open-world outpost.

It addresses the challenge by turning real NASA science into play. Kids manage Health, Air, Food, Radiation and Power, scrub dust off solar panels, grow crops, exercise in low gravity and shield against solar flares. The game uses real data from NASA's Curiosity RAD instrument, NASA DONKI and NASA OSDR, with an offline fallback.

This matters because radiation, oxygen and gravity are hard to understand from textbooks. Red Horizon makes them experiences with real consequences, sparking curiosity in the next generation of explorers. It runs in any browser with no install, built with React, TypeScript, Three.js, Tailwind CSS and Vite, using Antigravity, Google AI Studio and Claude.
details:
Red Horizon is an interactive 3D Moon and Mars outpost survival trainer for kids aged 7 to 12, built on real NASA science. Space topics like radiation, oxygen recycling and solar power are hard to picture in a textbook, so instead of reading about them, children live them as an astronaut.

HOW IT WORKS

The game opens with an 8-chapter 3D cutscene: Earth departure, rocket countdown and liftoff, an 8-month transit, Mars touchdown, a Sol 19 dust cyclone, and waking up alone on Mars. Five guided tutorial levels with live checklists then teach Air and Power management, dust storm sheltering, solar panel dust blackouts, solar flare shielding and rock sampling. After that, players enter a 150-Sol open-world survival mode and must repair the Lab Comms to 100% so a rescue shuttle can come home.

Players walk around a 3D outpost with a rover and a 12-panel solar farm, and can step inside the station and greenhouse. They scrub dust off solar panels with their mouse, grow crops, work out in the gym, run body scans and craft Anti-Rad Medkits. A top-left HUD tracks Health, Air, Food, Radiation and Power. The rules are real: 100% radiation or 0% health ends the mission, and low Martian gravity (0.38g) weakens muscles and bones unless the crew exercises.

REAL NASA SCIENCE

The game uses the Mars radiation level from NASA's Curiosity RAD instrument (about 0.67 mSv per day), solar flare data from NASA DONKI, and astronaut biology and space-farming themes from NASA OSDR. If the internet drops, it automatically falls back to built-in NASA archive data. Official NASA resources were used for the planets.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Children learn why space hazards matter by managing them, not by memorizing facts. The aim is to spark curiosity in the next generation of explorers. The game runs in any browser with no install or backend, so it works on a classroom laptop.

TOOLS

React 19, TypeScript, Three.js (3D terrain, base, crops and a .glb rover model), Tailwind CSS and Vite, and the Web Audio API. We built it with Antigravity, Google AI Studio and Claude, combined with our own ideas.

CREATIVITY

The audio is a big part of it. The game has 13 custom voiceovers and sound effects, plus a live synth soundtrack that speeds up during storms and flares. Dust storm wind is muffled when you step indoors.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Age-appropriate design: clean kid-friendly HUD, simple English, and one concept per tutorial level with Skip options. Scientific accuracy with real consequences, not fake progress bars. And accessibility, meaning offline fallback and no heavy hardware needed.
